newsitem.title: USA: Errors and slip-ups dogged police hunt for Cunanan.
newsitem.headline: Errors and slip-ups dogged police hunt for Cunanan.

text.p: In the aftermath of alleged multiple killer Andrew Cunanan's bloody rampage across the United States, which ended with his suicide on Wednesday, questions have arisen about police errors and slip-ups that may have cost fashion czar Gianni Versace his life.

A thumbprint left at a pawn shop, a chance sighting in a sandwich store and calls he tried to make on a victim's cellphone all hang in the air as tantalizing clues that could have led to his arrest before he allegedly shot Versace on July 15 at his oceanfront mansion in Miami Beach.

Yet Cunanan seemed to live a charmed life after he began what police say was a frantic killing spree in late April, allegedly battering friend Jeffrey Trail to death with a claw hammer in Minneapolis.
In the days before he allegedly shot Versace, Cunanan flirted with capture almost wilfully, as though daring FBI and police on his trail to find him.

The thumbprint -- together with his real name and address at a Miami Beach hotel -- sat unnoticed with piles of others at a police station for days after the pawn shop owner, following routine procudure, mailed it in.

An alert worker at a Miami Beach sandwich shop recognised him from an FBI 10 Most Wanted poster before the Versace slaying and called police, who asked him to delay serving Cunanan while officers rushed there.
Miami Beach Police Chief Richard Barreto said police responded to the call in eight minutes, but found Cunanan had slipped away after another employee served him.
In May, police believe Cunanan tried using the disabled car phone of his third alleged victim, real estate mogul Lee Miglin. Authorities picked up the signal but were unable to track the car down.

Local media speculated that Cunanan was monitoring the news and became aware that he could be tracked down via the car's cell phone. The next day, he is believed to have killed cemetery worker William Reese in New Jersey and abandoned the vehicle, stealing Reese's red pickup truck.
That truck sat for weeks in a Miami Beach parking garage. When police found it after Versace was shot, it contained Cunanan's passport inside as well as other clues linking him to past killings.
After the Versace killing, though, Cunanan's luck ran out. The attention friends said he craved reached international proportions, and there was nowhere left for him to go.
"We really put an unprecedented level of pressure on Andrew Cunanan," Barreto said. "The testament of that is he made it 40 blocks from the crime scene. I think he was a desperate man."
FBI Deputy Director William Esposito, at a news conference on Thursday, defended law enforcement agencies from criticism that they bungled a number of leads.

"You know, it's easy to look back and maybe criticise a certain office....If they had any leads, they were acting upon (them) as soon as possible. And again, you know, I'm not going to do any 20/20 hindsight," he said.

Esposito said an analysis of the investigation would be done to answer numerous questions, including, "What did we learn here? Is there something we can do better? And, if this happens again, what should we do different, if anything?"
Asked why the FBI did not know the pickup truck had been parked near Versace's mansion, he said:
"Why people didn't pick up on his vehicle in a parking garage is a good question. This was put out. We normally don't patrol parking garages."
Asked about the failure to check on the pawn ticket, Esposito said:

"Well, looking back on it, again, it's a very simple lead. But we had no information at the beginning of the manhunt that he had something that he was going to pawn. If we had known that, we probably would have flooded every pawn shop in the United States."
